AD MAXIM. CAESAREM tos a spasmo negare non possim. Item verbis et herbis fortisimis quodam aperuiffe feras mihi constat, quod neg; Dei virtute, neg; violenția rerum appofitarum exiftimo factum. Innumera quae vidi, & audivi possim introducere similia, quorum effectus manefi quid alhid, quam quaedam damo num miracula sunt denig; nonulli homines ni- min curiosi qui characteribus schedulis, annulis, figuris, monilibus, & vocabulis ignotis fidei et confidentiam pertinaciter adhibentes mirandos sapè confequuntur effectus, quos neg; sanctitas merito, neg; Dei conceffos miferatione, fed persida potius credulitate subminiftraffe diabolum mini- mè dubiramus. Daemones enim maximam humani generis inuidiam habentes, vt animas perdant mortalium, libenter occurrunt vanis operationibus impiorum. Quid nam sunt alhid characteres et occulorum interpretationes nominum, quam efculenta quaedam et potagia daemoniorum? Qui- cunque characteribus mirabiles effectus promitten- tibus, fidei adhibet, & fidei Chrifti et Ecclesiam sanctorum implicite negauit. Heu quor hodie Christiani, quot cleri, quot facerdotes (vt ma- ioribus parcam) superfitionibus et multis et variis vtuntur in actionibus quotidianis, quibus implicatas daemonum, sequuntur pastiones, in contumeliam Chriftiana fidei et propriam con- demnationem. Et quia haec mala iam nimium funt inter Christianos multiplicata, retraxit omnipotens manum, & tradixit eos in distio- nem perdiforud vt exaectores poenarum illos feniant, quorum imitatione non Deo viuo et vero, fed vanis superfitionibus pertinaciter militabunt. Suppo- 3: IOA, TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. Suppositione autem daemonum miranda fieri manifeste cognoscimus si diligentius veritatem inquirimus. Iudzini namq, Seraceni, Pagani sue gentiles qui non credunt in Deum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, si qua faciunt miracula, non Dei virtute, non angelorum ministerio, non sanctitatis merito, fed daemonum credimus suppositione facta. Nam quotiens omnipotentem Deum, in cuius vigenitum filium non credunt, pro aliquius mirandi effectus miferatione inuocant, iuens diabolus, quid non est peccatoribus falsus, & quia non exaudit altissimus peccatores infideles, vreos in errorib. conferunt. pertinaces, fe occulte pro Deo inuocato applicat, & fi potefi, permittente domino, quod postulatur orribus praefat. Hac diabolus suppositione tanto, liberius vitur, quanto minus a fide Christi et Ecclesia sacramenti simperditur. Manet enim ira Dei super omnes infideles, qui non credunt in eius vigenitum filium, & fuit in potestate diaboli. Ac ideo fe inuocatibus, ingreit in loco Dei. Vnde in suis errorib, obecati Dei innocens, in cuius filii no credut quos in ira manetis audire cui deficit, falsus miraculorur operator diabolus accedit. Credunt ergo iudificationibus diaboli, qui credere cotemunt veris miraculis Dei. A daemonib. falla miracula suis coenientia errorib. accipunt, qui veritatem, id est, Christi, sequi credendo no luerit. Multi fuit apud infideles, qui vnu Dei creatorum omnium colentes, idola non adorant et firmiter credunt in sua fe fide faluandos. Veru quia mysterium dominice incarnationis credere deficiunt, manet super eos ira Dei, & in suis fatuitatis bus euaneunt, exiftantes si Deum esse proximum, in quem non recte credunt fubliciturunt daemon.

To Emperor Maximilian

I cannot deny that [they were freed?] from a spasm. Likewise, I know that someone opened [locks?] by words and very powerful herbs; this I think was done neither by the power of God nor by the force of the things applied. I could bring forward countless similar things that I have seen and heard, whose effects, if they are manifest, are surely nothing other than certain miracles of demons. For some men, excessively curious, stubbornly placing faith and trust in characters, slips of paper, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, often obtain astonishing effects; these, we do not at all doubt, the devil has supplied, not by merit of holiness nor granted by God’s mercy, but rather through treacherous credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, readily come to meet the vain operations of the impious, in order to destroy the souls of mortals. What else are characters and interpretations of hidden names than certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever places faith in characters promising marvelous effects has implicitly denied both the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints. Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to spare greater men, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions, by which they follow the entangled passions of demons, to the disgrace of the Christian faith and to their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied too greatly among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and handed them over into the power of destroyers, so that they may feel as exactors of punishments those whom, by imitation, they will stubbornly have served, not the living and true God, but vain superstitions.

3: The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius

By the substitution of demons, moreover, we know plainly, if we inquire more diligently into the truth, that astonishing things are done. For the Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in God our Lord Jesus Christ, if they perform any miracles, we believe that these are done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by merit of holiness, but by the substitution of demons. For whenever they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for mercy in regard to some marvelous effect, then the devil, coming in, who is not false to sinners, and because the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, in order that they may persist in errors, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked and, if he can, the Lord permitting, grants to [their] prayers what is requested. The devil uses this substitution the more freely, the less he is hindered by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son, and [he] was in the power of the devil. And therefore he enters, for those invoking him, in the place of God. Hence, blinded in their errors, while the innocent God, in whose Son they do not believe, fails to hear those remaining in wrath, the devil comes as a false worker of miracles. Therefore those who scorn believing the true miracles of God believe the deceits of the devil. They receive from demons false miracles suited to their errors, those who, by believing, have not chosen to follow the truth, that is, Christ. There have been many among the unbelievers who, worshiping the one God, creator of all things, do not adore idols and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they fail to believe the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them; and in their follies they vanish away, thinking that God is near, in whom they do not rightly believe; [they are] subjected to the demon.

AD MAXIM. CAESAREM. nibus, quorum falsis miraculis fidem adhibentes in suis errorib. mendacio confirmantur. Cuius rei si- militudinem introduxisse ô Caesar non pigeat: E-rat homo quidam custos porcorum qui schedulam bacillo incluserat nomen diui martyris Blasij continentem, cui tantum fidei detulit, baculo in me-dio gregis terrae affixo, lupum ab accessu prohib-itum crederat omnem. Hac stulta confidentia per longam experientiam tandem roborata, ibat homo securus quocunque volebat, dimittens sine periculo in nemore porcos, cum luporum iam nullus habe-ret accessum, contigit pertransire videntem ab-sente pastore, qui cernens daemones custodiam habere gregis dixit ad eum, quid miser hic agis? qui respondit, istos custodio porcos, at ille, quis tibi curam porcorum commisit? iterum respondit: stulta confidentia pastoris, nam schedulam quan-dam bacillo inclusam magnae putatesse virtutis, qui Blasij cuiusdam meritis lupi arceantur â portis, su-am peccauit in legem nostras sequitur vanitates, verum quia inuocatus non comparet, ego, ne ho-mo confidentiam suam amitteret porcos eius cu- stodio, me pro Blasio libens suppono. Ita inquit mortales vanis coniurationibus nos molestant, vt nisi velimus aestimationem nostri honorem a-pud eos perdere omnem, necesse fit eorum inuoca-tionibus stultis plerumque occurramus. Huius simili-tudine facti daemones miseros infideles decipiunt, miracula quae orantes à Deo postulant, malignorum spirituum suppositione saepius af-se-quuntur. In his enim quae Dei vel cultum respici-unt vel honorem, libenter se daemones ingerunt, qui manifestos honores assequi nequeunt, occul-tis nimirum delectantur. C Simul 34 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. Simul notandum, quod ab initio mundi nulli vn- quam religioni vel sectae principaliter excellenti defuere miracula; quamuis non omnia ex vno princi- pio sint facta. Nã quicquid miraculorũ in vera reli- gione factum est, non aliunde quam adeò factum est. Habuit enim lex naturae miracula sua, habuit lex scripta, habuit iam simul et gratia. Qui religio- nem dedit omnipotens Deus, ipse etiam miracula facit. In falsis autem religionibus vbi veritas non colitur, si qua fiunt miracula, non Deus sed diabo- lus operatur. Deus enim cum fit veritas, religiones falsas non instituit, & ideo suis miraculis nunquam mẽdacium illustrauit. Mahumet qui malo daemone plenus, falsam religionem instituit, non ex Deo, sed cooperatione daemonum falsis eam miraculis exornauit. Daemon etenim, qui causam dedit er- roris, etiam miraculum (occasione tamen accepta:) falsum potuit exhibere deceptis. Vnde si Mahume- to nouam religionem rudi populo persuadenti pe- nitus defuissent miracula, nemo ei forsitan adhibu- isset fidem. Ostendit enim et ipse tam subtilitate ingenij quam cooperatione diaboli quaedã miranda populis, vt nouam doctrinam nous quoque mira- culis confirmasse videretur. Paganis idololatris e- tiam non defuerunt miracula, si fidem historijs non negamus. Iudaei verò ante incarnationem filij Dei legem eius suscipientes per Mosen diuinis frequen- ter miraculis fuerunt illustrati. At verò post do- minicam resurrectionem euacuata lege Mosaica, qui non credunt in vnigenitum filium Dei manent sub ira indignationis eius, & cessauerunt ab eis om- nia miracula veritatis. Vnde si qua hodie miranda faciunt, daemonum sunt opera et manifesti indicia erroris. Maximè enim demonẽs studio inuihilant, vt cos

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear], in whose false miracles, when they place faith, they are confirmed by falsehood in their errors. It should not displease us, O Caesar, to introduce an analogy for this matter. There was a certain swineherd who had enclosed in his staff a little slip containing the name of the holy martyr Blasius; he ascribed so much trust to it that, when the staff was fixed in the ground in the midst of the herd, he believed every wolf was kept from coming near. When this foolish confidence had at last been strengthened by long experience, the man went safely wherever he wished, leaving the pigs in the wood without danger, since no wolf now had any access. It happened that one passing by saw this in the shepherd’s absence; and, observing that demons were keeping guard over the herd, he said to one of them: “What are you doing here, wretch?” He answered: “I am guarding these pigs.” But the other said: “Who entrusted you with the care of the pigs?” Again he answered: “The shepherd’s foolish confidence. For, thinking a certain slip enclosed in a staff to be of great power, by which through the merits of some Blasius wolves are kept from the gates, he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities. But since the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his pigs, and willingly put myself in the place of Blasius.” Thus, he says, mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we wish to lose all esteem and honor for ourselves among them, it often becomes necessary for us to answer their foolish invocations. By the likeness of this event demons deceive wretched unbelievers: the miracles which they ask of God in prayer they very often obtain through the substitution of malignant spirits. For in those things which concern either the worship or the honor of God, demons readily insert themselves; since they cannot obtain open honors, they plainly take delight in hidden ones.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

At the same time it must be noted that, from the beginning of the world, miracles have never been lacking to any religion or sect of principal excellence, although not all have been done from one principle. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no other source than from God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had them; grace now has them likewise. Almighty God, who gave religion, himself also works miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, not God but the devil works them. For since God is truth, he did not institute false religions, and therefore he has never adorned a lie with his miracles. Muhammad, who was full of an evil demon and instituted a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God, but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of error could also, when the occasion had been accepted, display a false miracle to the deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Muhammad when he was persuading a rude people of a new religion, perhaps no one would have given him credence. For he too showed the peoples certain marvels, both by subtlety of intellect and by the cooperation of the devil, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine with new miracles as well. Miracles were not lacking even to the pagan idolaters, if we do not deny credence to the histories. The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illumined by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been emptied of force, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if today they do any marvelous things, they are works of demons and manifest indications of error. For demons labor especially with zeal to

Cernimus enim in his qui plerumque amoris interni ad Iesum desiderio carnis modum contemplantes excedunt â terra sursum leuatos in aẽra, quos non sua dunctaxat acie mentis, sed diuina nihil ominus virtute pondus exedere corporale putamus. Tria igitur memorata opinionis principia incognita multis satisfaciunt mea sententia paucis, vt mens in corpore posita rem dico expertam. Cum profequerer adolescens studia literarum, in vno lecto quatuor eramus nocte quadam dormientes, furrexit è latere meo coaevus et dormiens vt solebat in somnis oculis clausis et luna introlucente quinta decima, quasi vigil circumambulabat, ascendit muros, & ciurum agilitate sua vincebat, lectum quoque secundo et tertio sopitus transcendit, caleauit nos pedibus omnes, nec magis sensimus pondus, quam simus nos contigisset exiguum. Quocunque dormiens corpus mouebatur subitò ianuarium omnes vltra aperiebantur clausurae. Altiora domus, aedificia velocissimè penetrauit et more passeris hęrebat in tectis. Visa loquor nõ va ga relatione audita. Haec animae nõ corporis videtur officia, quae sua naturali potestate, vt ita dixerrim, quasi liberè vtitur, quando ligatis sensibus carnis extra domicilium corporis euagatur. Sed cum non fit propositae quaestioni, materia ex omni parte conueniens, de causis horum mirabilium in aliud D D

To Maximilian Caesar.

those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they make, by the continuance of fraud, obstinate in error even to death. For indeed, when God for just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unrecognized; and, seeing that salvation is far away, he seduces the minds of the ignorant by false miracles, as though the Lord were near. Therefore whatever miracles belong to unbelievers are works of demons. For just as outside the unity of the Christian faith there is no salvation for mortals, so without Christ the most holy power of wonders is not granted. For now demons, lurking in ambush, long since conquered and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the incarnation of the Lord, and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also those who add a fourth to the three modes set down above, saying that the mind or spirit of the man himself can naturally do wondrous things, provided it knows how to recall itself from everything adventitious into itself, above the senses, into unity. For those who ascribe such things to nature promise that it can do wonders, foretell the future, disclose the secrets of men, remove diseases, and suddenly change a man’s counsels. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, something I have not experienced, it is necessary that some external power also come in and that either a good angel or an evil spirit in part occupy the one thinking. But if no external powers intermingle, the one prophesying must form his beginning either from conjectures or from a bold presumption of speaking, and pronounce a judgment sometimes true, sometimes false. For indeed, as long as the spirit dwells in the body, by its nature it naturally understands nothing without the service of the senses.

The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius.

Hence I would not altogether resist, if they grant that our confused and crude understanding is aided by a like service. For we see in the case of those who very often, through the desire of inward love for Jesus, pass in contemplation beyond the measure of the flesh, that they are lifted upward from the earth into the air; and we think that they overcome the bodily weight not merely by their own keenness of mind, but no less by divine power. Therefore the three aforementioned principles of opinion, unknown to many, satisfy, in my judgment, few, as the mind is placed in the body. I speak of a thing experienced. When as a young man I was pursuing the studies of letters, four of us were sleeping in one bed on a certain night. One of my own age rose from my side and, asleep as he was accustomed to be in dreams, with eyes closed and with the moon on its fifteenth day shining in, walked about as if awake; he climbed walls and surpassed a squirrel in his agility. While asleep he also crossed over the bed a second and a third time; he trod on all of us with his feet, and we felt his weight no more than if a tiny mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, suddenly all the fastenings of doors opened of themselves. He very swiftly penetrated the higher buildings of the house and clung to the roofs in the manner of a sparrow. I speak of things seen, not heard by vague report. These seem to be functions of the soul, not of the body; the soul uses its natural power, so to speak, almost freely, when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling of the body. But since the matter does not in every respect suit the proposed question, concerning the causes of these wonders to another

Multa enim ad perfectionem fidei sunt necessaria quae in diuinis scripturis non reperiuntur sufficienter expressa. Ad hanc maiestatis tuae sacratissimae quaestionem videtur respondendum, omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata perfectum diuinitatis est opus, ante tem- pus omne ordinatum praeordinatum, in tempore scriptum, non secus quam Deus voluit, qui vt scri- beretur hominibus inspirauit. Dei enim omnia per- fecta sunt opera: Ideoque cum scriptura, de qua lo- quimur, Dei fit opus: Necessarium est eam in omni- bus confiteri perfectam. Summus etenim arbiter Deus, cuius omnia perfecta sunt opera, sicut voluit et amp; quem voluit scripturis suis ordinem contulit, &amp; excipientibus illas quemadmodum scriberent pro- cul dubio infudit. Sacrae nãque scripturę tantam om- nipotens Deus authoritatem et amp; maiestatem contu- lit, vt in eius comparatione omnia huius mundi vo- cabula deficiant, cum diuina humanis propriè ne- queant comprehendi sermonibus, Diuina igitur scriptura quę superficie verborum nescientibus ap- paret confluâ, scientibus eam videtur manifesta, quoniam nisi legatur illo spiritu, quo influâ homi- nibus creditur, ad eius intellectum minimè perue- nitur. Aliter eam legit doctus, qui carnis embracu- lo ac vanis desiderijs aestuat, &amp; aliter intelligens, quem exutum voluptatibus, amor Dei veraciter in- flammat. Vnde mirum non est, si homines carnali- ter sapientes diuinas scripturas non intelligent, qui carnis voluptatibus obcecati Dei spiritus dulcedi- nem nem ro pri hibea libelle ram, i bin.Pa rum s piente vicips et amp; in non passi ne be Surgy vitz f runt, j quam nuclae tiua tuin men hab ver tū ruo scrip num nis,c̃e Papa mõdi qvon tum modi mylɔ nulo

[unclear]

To Emperor Maximilian.

But let us defer the discussion to another time. For we do not believe that these things are wonders to wise men, who have understood very well the power and nobility of the human mind, since, hindered only by the interposition of the body, it is in some respect reckoned equal to the angels. Finally, I pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which a frenzied person produces very wondrous effects upon external things. The very strong imagination of a confident person can also do much toward producing wonderful effects, whether upon a true object or upon one merely supposed.

Therefore, since there are so many kinds and modes of working wonders, it is no wonder if Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and all other unbelievers established outside the faith of Christ, who cannot perform miracles through public justice, enact wonders either by the support of demons or by artful industry. Nor does it escape me that, by the same reasoning, the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as if they were not done by the power of the Creator, but rather by the entanglement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that the miracles of all unbelievers have been accomplished by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and stubbornly thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture.

Question Four.

The fourth question of your Most Serene Majesty was this: why almighty God did not give Holy Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith, of both the New and the Old Testament, as open and manifest, uniform in all things, and plainly sufficient for all things, but rather as wrapped up and, in many places, full of riddles. For many things necessary for the perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

To this question of your Most Sacred Majesty it seems that one must answer: every Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity, ordered and preordained before all time, written in time in no other way than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. For all the works of God are perfect. And therefore, since the Scripture of which we speak is the work of God, it is necessary to confess that it is perfect in all things. For God, the supreme judge, whose works are all perfect, gave to his Scriptures the order he willed and the one he willed, and without doubt infused into those receiving them how they should write. For almighty God bestowed such authority and majesty upon Sacred Scripture that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended in human speech. Therefore divine Scripture, which on the surface of its words appears confused to the ignorant, seems manifest to those who know it, because unless it is read in that spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into men, one by no means arrives at its understanding. The learned man who burns with the embrace of the flesh and with vain desires reads it in one way, and the understanding man, whom the love of God truly inflames after he has been stripped of pleasures, reads it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men wise according to the flesh do not understand the divine Scriptures, who, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, the sweetness of the Spirit of God [unclear].

AD MAXIM. CAESAREM. nem, nunquam perceperunt. Quemadmodũ si pue- ro prima literarum elementa discenti, volumen ex- hibeas quodcunque scriptùm, cuius character suo fit libello dissimilis, cum legere nequiuerit scriptu- ram, ilico malam non rectè formatam exclama- bit. Parì modo ad lectionem diuinarum scriptura- rum accedentes homines, carnaliter duntaxat sa- pientes, que ea qui diuini spiritus sunt non capiunt, vicijs temeritate grauij, cum suam ignorantiam indignitatem culpàre debuissent, scripturas quas non intelligunt sanctas repraehendunt. Non enim pasim õnibus diuinas licet interpretari scripturas, ne bestia, contingens montẽ, lapidibus obruatur. Surgunt nunc ordine praepostero plures, qui omne vitae suae tempus in literis humanitatis consumpsē- runt, seniores facti diuinas scripturas, quas nun- quam didicerunt, perperam interpretantes, non e- nuclarent sed confundunt in proprio sensu discu- tiunt. Vnde quicunque sacras scripturas non eo spiri- tu intelligunt, quo scribentibus sunt infusa, vela- men ignorantiae temeritatis super cordibus suis habent, more Iudaeorum expanse, inde saepius venenum pernitio si erroris hauriunt, vnde in spiri- tu accedentes Dei humiles salutis poculum accepē- runt. Non enim habetur doctrina caelestis in verbis scripturarum, sed in sensu, non in superficie sermo- num, sed in intellectu, non in folijs ornatae oratio- nis, sed in occulto mystice inspirationis. Hinc diuis Papa Gregorius, sacra inquit scriptura omnes huius mũdi scientias more locutionis suae lõgè transcẽdit quoniam in uno eodemque sermonem dum narrat tex- tum, occultum prodit mysterium, quemad- modum simplices superficie refouet, ita sapientes mysterio exercet, habet enim in publico vnde par- nulos nutriat seruat in occulto, vnde mentes C4 subli: 40 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. sublimium in admirationem dulcedinis suspendat, quasi fluuius quidam mirabilis in quo et agnus sim- plex paruulus ambulet elephas magnus natet. Et S. Augustinus super Genesin dicit: Sic diuina lo- quitur scriptura, vt altitudine sua superbos irri- deat, attentos profunditate sua terreat, magnos vir- tute pascat, sua paruulos affabilitate nutriat. Ma- ior est enim sacrae scripturae autoritas, quam fit om- nis ingenij humani perspicacitas. Propterea quate- nus ad earum verum intellectum perueniatur, in- primis purgandus est ab omni affectione carnali a- nimus, implorandum sedulò cum humilitate diui- nae bonitatis auxiliũ, vt suo illuminet spiritu discẽ- tis intellectũ. Autoritati namque diuinarũ scripturarũ omnia colla subdenda sunt potestatum. Et sicut diu- us inquit Hieronimus, nunquam fic adulandum est homini, vt sanctarum scripturarũ veritas negliga- tur, quae tota in vtroque testamento in narratione gestorum est vera, in monitionibus recta, in pro- missionibus certa, in comminationibus terribili- ter metuenda. Quocirca non omnibus datum est posse diuinarum scripturarum penetrare mysteria, sed illis duntaxat vtcumque permittitur quibus a- mor continuat studium, Dei spiritus purgatis mentibus verum confert intellectum. Quisquis au- tem caligine viciorum est sordidus, quisquis men- te tumida incedit superbus. Quisquis de veritate scripturarum Dei vel in parte vel in toto dubitat nunquam ad earum intelligentiam se posse pertin- gere confidat. Dicit enim ipsius auctoritas scriptu- rae quod nisi credideritis non intelligetis. Nostri est tarditas ingenij, nostri quoque impuritas desiderij quoties diuinas scripturas non rectè intelligimus, quando videlicet velamen pernitiosae occupationis super

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] they have never perceived. Just as, if you show to a boy learning the first elements of letters any written volume whose character is unlike that in his own little book, when he cannot read the writing he will at once cry out that it is bad and not properly formed. In the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures, wise only in a fleshly manner, and who do not grasp those things that are of the divine Spirit, burdened by vices and rashness, when they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach as holy the Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not lawful for everyone everywhere to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast, touching the mountain, be overwhelmed with stones.

Many now arise in a reversed order, who have spent the whole time of their life on humane letters; having become older men, they wrongly interpret the divine Scriptures, which they have never learned, and do not explain them but confuse them, examining them according to their own sense. Hence all who do not understand the sacred Scriptures by that Spirit by which they were breathed into those who wrote them have over their hearts the veil of ignorance and rashness, spread out after the manner of the Jews; from there they very often drink the poison of destructive error, from which those who approach humbly in the Spirit of God have received the cup of salvation.

For heavenly doctrine is not contained in the words of the Scriptures, but in their meaning; not on the surface of the words, but in the understanding; not in the leaves of ornate speech, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in the manner of its speech, since in one and the same discourse, while it recounts the text, it reveals a hidden mystery; just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has in public that from which it may nourish little ones; it preserves in secret that by which it may suspend the minds of the lofty in wonder at its sweetness, like a certain marvelous river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

And St. Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its strength it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones. For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the perspicacity of human talent. Therefore, in order that one may come to their true understanding, above all the mind must be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the aid of divine goodness must be diligently implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illumine the understanding of the learner.

For all necks of powers must be subjected to the authority of the divine Scriptures. And, as the divine Jerome says, one must never flatter a man in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected; in the whole of both Testaments it is true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terrifyingly to be feared in its threats. Therefore it has not been given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but it is permitted in some measure only to those in whom love makes study continuous, and to whose purified minds the Spirit of God grants true understanding.

But whoever is foul with the darkness of vices, whoever walks with a swollen mind, proud; whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God, whether in part or in whole, let him never trust that he can attain to their understanding. For the authority of Scripture itself says that unless you have believed, you will not understand. The slowness of our talent is ours, and so too the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures, namely when the veil of pernicious occupation

Si autem ex hominib. est, quarẽ vos promissam in ea salutem speratis aeternã? quam homo dare non potest. Nisi forsitan pergatis dicere insani conficta omnia, &amp; nihil restare post fa- taquam cineré, mētemque simul cum corpore subire interi-

To Maximilian Caesar.

... remains spread over our hearts, which does not permit us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the sense which the Holy Spirit has poured into the divine Scriptures, but, seizing the bare words of the writers, we twist them into another sense. Indeed, if our minds were purged of carnal vices, if through the continual pursuit of sobriety the intellect were stirred up in the Scriptures, if belief and reverence were applied as their dignity requires, every student would understand more clearly than light that in the sacred readings there is nothing confused, nothing misshapen, nothing unsuitable, nothing absurd, or inserted without the most just reason. For all the passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; and whenever anything in them seems to have been set down obscurely, this has been done by divine providence, so that the studious mind may have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple may not lose the place of due reverence. Therefore not by chance, but by eternal providence, he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that it might abound in as many mysteries as senses in which, by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, it is explained in Catholic fashion by the doctors. For, as holy Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it begets many meanings of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; for when one man draws out this sense, and another that sense, while expounding it in Catholic fashion, it becomes known how lofty and deep it is. Therefore let no man swollen with secular learning suppose that he understands sacred Scripture, unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning is of more value for exercising the intellect than for illuminating the understanding toward true wisdom. Therefore without doubt divine Scripture is, to minds purified through the continual exercise of the fear of God and frequent study of reading, both manifest and clear, though to filthy minds, confused by secular wisdom, it seems obscure.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection, being frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote. For if they are read in another spirit than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must necessarily be wholly shut away from true understanding. But when we encounter some discordance in them, let us understand that it is only of words, not of meanings; and it arises not by chance but by the ordering providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures, may be strengthened and not become altogether sluggish. For the counsel of God cannot be deceived; but the divine Scriptures were written by the counsel of his will. It follows necessarily that they are true and in no way false. They were men by whom the divine [Scriptures] came to us. You who are devoted to secular wisdom, say of the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, which the Church of Christians has received and venerates as true, authentic, and holy Scripture: whence do you believe it was received, from God or from men? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks the Scripture which he believes to be inspired most openly resists the divine ordering. But if it is from men, why do you hope for the eternal salvation promised in it, which man cannot give? Unless perhaps, madmen, you go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that nothing remains after fate except ashes, and that the mind together with the body undergoes

Cum ergo scriptura sacra perfectum fit Dei opus, fic mentem confirmemus Caelar oportet, quatenus eam credamus veram, re- ctam, integram, solidam, diuinitus inspiratam omnibus ad Christianae fidei confirmationem intel- ligentibus abundantissimè sufficientem. Enimuerò nisi diuina scriptura, vera, sancta, perfectaque in om- nibus credatur integra, fundamento suo fides priuaretur Christiana. Cauendum est ergò maximè omni Christiano ne plus quam expedit diuinas dif- cutiendo scripturas terminos egrediatur pietatis, quia non homo auctor est scripturarum, sed spiri- tus sanctus cuius ordinationi refistere conuincitur, quisquis integritati scripturarum Dei reluctatur. Est autem scriptura (ordinante Deo) parabolis, ae- nigmatibus, similitudinibusque cõparationibus v- tiliter intexta figurarum, quatenus legentes exerci- tentur ad intelligentiam, interna dulcedine gustata, mens confirmetur ad pietatẽ. Itaque si pu- rificatis mentibus fensum attendamus scripturam̃ non verba, intelligemus quam rectè propriè om- nia fint ordinata. Non enim decebat facras scriptu- ras, in quibus cognitio diuinae traditur maiestatis, vsque adeò plenas esse manifestas, vt passim intel- ligerentur ab omnibus que bonis intelligenda dun- taxat proponitur sanctis nō etiā malis fordidisque mentibus atque pollutis. Hinc etenim scriptum est: bestia quae tetigerit montes lapidibus obruatur. Quid hic designatur per bestiam? nisi homines imi- tatione brutorum fine Dei amore viuentes in vo- luptatibus

To Maximilian Caesar

destruction, a profession which would show you to be no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit; but if, having fallen with the apostates into a reprobate sense, you say that they were [composed?] by men, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness, and you openly reveal yourselves to be unskilled and rash judges, since you condemn Scripture which you do not understand. But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind longer against the rashness of emperors. This one thing I want you to know: that no one understands unless he receives; but because you set the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, therefore you do not have the understanding of true wisdom. For almighty God deigns, through grace, to be present as illuminator to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except for God. The Spirit of God brings help by his presence to those whom he has found rooted in the love of truth, and, having been cleansed from every extraneous thing, he leads them into the knowledge of all things. For to those who truly love God all things are open, all things naked, all things manifest, since whoever, through love, beholds in the faith of Jesus Christ him who creates and governs all things, knows all things that are necessary for his salvation. But, on the contrary, the illumination of God dwells very far from the slothful, the wicked, gluttons, the envious, the avaricious, [incubonibus], the filthy, the lustful, murderers, the impious, the proud, and those alien to piety, leaving them to the discretion of the avenging demon, who, driving in the sharp point of savage fire, afflicts sense and mind, and more and more arms and drives the impious to perpetrate crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also be liable to a sharper punishment.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

Whence, entangled in vices and worldly desires, they not only cannot penetrate the divine Scriptures with understanding, but, neglecting themselves, do not even know themselves. Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is the perfect work of God, we must so confirm the mind, Caesar, that we believe it true, right, complete, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith. Indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect, and complete in all things, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Therefore every Christian must take the greatest care that, by scrutinizing the divine Scriptures more than is expedient, he not go beyond the bounds of piety, because the author of the Scriptures is not man, but the Holy Spirit; and whoever resists the integrity of God’s Scriptures is proved to resist his ordinance. Moreover Scripture, by God’s ordaining, is usefully interwoven with parables, enigmas, likenesses, and comparisons of figures, so that readers may be exercised toward understanding and, once the inward sweetness has been tasted, the mind may be confirmed in piety. And so, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of Scripture, not the words, we shall understand how rightly and properly all things have been ordered. For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which the knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so completely full and manifest that they would everywhere be understood by all; what is proposed to be understood is only for the good and holy, not also for evil, filthy, and polluted minds. Hence indeed it is written: “the beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” What is designated here by the beast, if not men who, in imitation of brute animals, live without the love of God in pleasures

26
AD MAXIM. CAESAREM. 45 luptatibus carnis. Et quid per montem exprimitur, nisi diuinarum altitudo scripturarum.Accedens ad montem hunc sanctum bestia lapidibus obruitur, quoniã homo mẽte impurus , aut circa fidem infir- mus, qui altitudinem scripturarum diuinarum ri- mari sine tradente magistro nititur, varijs &; perni- ciosis erroribus quasi lapidum ictibus vulneratur. Nam sicut omnia munda sunt mundis, ita prophana videntur cuncta prophanis. Posuit ergo Deus lati- bulum suum altitudinem scripturarum quae sic in- accessibilis, &; clausa est reprobis vt tamen sem- per manifesta pateat sanctis. Quare autem omnipotens Deus scripturam san- ctam ad omnia, quae fidem respiciunt Christianam, non dederit sufficientem &; manifestam, breuiter respondemus. Duo sunt, quae ad confirmationem fidei Christianae altissimus prouidit credentibus, Ecclesiam videlicet &; scripturam, vt quod in altera de- claretur.Vnde si quid in scripturis sanctis circa re- gulas fidei minus sufficienter inuenimus expressũ, mox recursum habemus ad Ecclesiam, Et vbi Eccle- sia in formatione salutari opus habet ad pietatem illico se confert ad scripturam. neque fine scriptura haberet Ecclesię autoritatem, neque si- ne Ecclesia fidem scriptura, vt duorum fiat senten- tiavna.Augustinus enim dicit: Euangelio non cre- derem, nisi auctoritas Ecclesię me compelleret.Io. annes autem Gersonensis dicit: Ecclesię non crede- rem, nisi Euangelium me compelleret.Confirmat autem scripturam santam Ecclesia, &; ipsa confir- matur pariformiter â scriptura,Ecclesia abundat quoties scriptura deficit.Et si quando Ecclesia du- bitat,ad scripturae consilium recurrit.Vnus enim est 46 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. est Dei spiritus sanctus, qui in fide Iesu Christi fundauit Ecclesiam, ipse idem omnipotens qui so- lus inspirauit scripturam. Et hic est funiculus tri- plex, qui non facile rumpitur, vbi scriptura diuina per spiritum sanctum authoritate Ecclesiae copula- tur vsque adeo vt Ecclesia scripturam, & scriptura rursus commendet Ecclesiam. Causam itaque vt mi- hi videtur ad propositam quaestionem inuictae ma- iestatis ô Caesar sufficientem assignauimus. Quo- niam si omnia in scripturis sanctis essent manife- ste expressa, quae pietatem fidei respiciunt, non vi- deretur tantae authoritatis sapcta mater Ecclesia, & euacuaretur magna ex parte meritum obedi- entiae salutaris. Simul ad principalem quaestionem satis puto responsum, vbi quidam existimant, scripturam sacram in plerisque locis esse confusam et amp; imperfectam, quam tamen, si debita mentis pu- ritate legerent, inuenirent vtique perfectam et amp; so- lidam. Authoritas Ecclesiae Catholicae magna est, quae sola in his quae fidem respiciunt in dubijs ha- bet interpraetari scripturas cui omnium subiicien- da sunt colla potestatum â cuius diffinitione si quis ausu temerario discesserit, Euangelium Christi ne- gauit. Vna est fidelium congregatio mater Christia- norum, Ecclesia sancta, extra cuius vnitatem nemo saluabitur, quae etsi in moribus quandoque vi- deatur infirma, tamen fide semper con- stans nunquam errauit Christi pietate salua. * * * DE RE-

To Maximilian Caesar.

pleasures of the flesh. And what is expressed by the mountain, if not the height of the divine Scriptures? When a beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a man impure in mind, or weak in regard to the faith, who strives to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a teacher handing it down, is wounded by various and pernicious errors as by blows of stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane. Therefore God placed his hiding-place in the height of the Scriptures, which is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that nevertheless it always lies manifestly open to the saints.

But why almighty God did not give Holy Scripture as sufficient and manifest for all things that concern the Christian faith, we answer briefly. There are two things that the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith, namely the Church and Scripture, so that what is declared in one may be supplied in the other. Hence if we find anything in the Holy Scriptures concerning the rules of faith expressed less sufficiently, we at once have recourse to the Church; and where the Church, in saving instruction, has need of help for piety, it immediately betakes itself to Scripture. Nor would the Church have authority without Scripture, nor Scripture faith without the Church, so that from the two there may be one judgment. For Augustine says: I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me. But Johannes Gersonensis says: I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me. The Church confirms Holy Scripture, and it likewise is confirmed by Scripture. The Church abounds whenever Scripture is lacking. And if at any time the Church is in doubt, it has recourse to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God, who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ, the very same almighty one who alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord, which is not easily broken, where divine Scripture is joined by the Holy Spirit to the authority of the Church to such a degree that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church.

Thus, as it seems to me, O Caesar of unconquered majesty, we have assigned a sufficient reason for the question proposed. For if all things that concern the piety of faith were manifestly expressed in the Holy Scriptures, holy mother Church would not appear to be of such great authority, and the merit of saving obedience would in large part be emptied away. At the same time I think a sufficient answer has been given to the principal question, where certain people suppose Sacred Scripture in very many places to be confused and imperfect; yet if they read it with due purity of mind, they would indeed find it perfect and solid. Great is the authority of the Catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning the faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures; to it the necks of all powers must be subjected. If anyone by rash daring departs from its definition, he has denied the Gospel of Christ. There is one congregation of the faithful, the mother of Christians, the holy Church; outside its unity no one will be saved. And although in morals it may sometimes seem weak, nevertheless in faith it has always remained constant and has never erred, by the preserving mercy of Christ.

To Emperor Maximilian 47

On the Reprobate and Witches

Fifth Question

The fifth question of Your Most Serene Highness was this: Why can impious, evil, and reprobate persons in matters of faith, such as those women whom we commonly call witches, command malignant spirits, when good men, and the most zealous observers of the Christian faith, can neither command good spirits nor always malignant ones?

I remember that I formerly answered this question as follows: In all the works of the divine majesty there is an order and sequence of beauty, of immovable equity, by which individual things, suitably disposed, persevere in the rank which they have received. For without its proper order nothing subsists. In the world, in this order, the freedom of will which the Creator gave to all human beings is driven by no violence of power so as not always to remain in the order which the first man received from the beginning of his creation. Hence no one among mortals is good except by the counsel of his own will, assisted by the grace of a merciful God; and no one is evil except of his own accord, deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin. By rectitude of will we are made like good spirits, if we prove the piety of the faith which we have in Christ by holy and necessary works. And just as the consummation of a good will makes good men equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious renders them like demons. Hence evil and perverse people, the more they have been depraved by the malice of their own will,

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions 48

the more they become like demons in disposition. By likeness, moreover, the familiarity of friendship is introduced, from which mutual confidence is gradually generated. From the confidence of the lesser toward the greater, command arises, whether it is true or feigned by cunning. Therefore, if there seems to be any command of wicked people over demons, it arises from the greatness of their wickedness: namely, when their disposition is depraved to such a degree that, by a reprobate will, they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons joining with them.

For demons are not all equal in malice or intelligence; rather, one is much more cunning than another in quickness of understanding, and far worse in depraved affection. For those who, having fallen from the high seats, dwell nearer the earth and inhabit caverns and caves, are certainly duller than the rest, to such a degree that they fear swords and rods, and seem to be moved by the threats of men who terrify them. This may be observed in those whom we call energumens. But demons who dwell farther removed from the earth are subtler by nature and meet with human beings more rarely. People full of malice, however, the more they advance in perversity of will, the more like demons they become; admitted by them into familiarity, they thereafter become bold, and receive command over the demons whose familiarity they use: a command not of violence, but of pretense. For demons, in order to keep willing in their depravity those people whom they have once received into surrender, gladly subject themselves to them, as though moved by a feigned dominion; what they do voluntarily, they pretend that they are compelled to do in obedience. For no one obtains true command over demons except one whom faith in the Lord [unclear].

To Maximilian Caesar.

... has made our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, acceptable and a friend to God; for thus Scripture says of those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.” Evil men therefore command demons, whom malice has made like to them; likeness made them familiar, and familiarity made them their own and subject.

It is as if some servant, born in a humble station, were said to command a great prince, which often happens, because he has been joined to him by long familiarity; through this he obtains without contradiction everything he has asked, so that he seems rather to rule his lord than to be ruled by him. According to this likeness, evil and reprobate men, who are admitted by demons into their familiarity and become very bold through more prolonged [unclear] confidence, receive a counterfeit, not to say familiar, command over them, which they have deserved by the likeness of a most depraved will. Hence whatever they have sought to receive from demons for themselves by an explicit compact, with [unclear] concurring, they receive, except whenever, being forbidden by divine ordinance, they are unable to furnish what is asked. Yet they do not thus present themselves indiscriminately to all reprobate and evil persons, but only to those with whom, through the intervention of some compact, they have entered into treaties, as are sorcerous women who have done homage to the Devil, and invokers of those same demons, whom the common people call by the customary term necromancers.

There are two kinds of men who may command lawfully.

The first indeed is of those men who, beloved of God by the merit of holiness, have received from him the power of trampling the head of the ancient serpent, such as in the primitive Church were the Apostles and their followers and disciples, concerning whom the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they will cast out demons,” and “they will take up serpents.”

The second kind, however, is of those men to whom, by reason of their order in the Church of God, it is granted that they drive demons out of men’s bodies by the power of the ministry received. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God, namely when they are ordained by the bishop.

Again there are two kinds of men who desire to command demons; with what unlawful presumption they do this, they show by their most wicked conditions.

The first and most pernicious kind is that of sorceresses, who enter into pacts with demons and, after a solemn profession has first been made, hand themselves over to some demon as property and for perpetual service. How many evils this most pernicious kind of human beings commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, there is no one who can express. For first of all, denying God and the faith of Christ and holy Baptism, they offer themselves, in mind and body, to demons; by their sorcery they make human beings and beasts sick, harm them, and kill them. There is no disease which, if God permits it, they cannot bring on, because, when they present themselves as servants to demons in observance of the compacted treaty, by comparison with them they dare whatever they wish. Hence they are nowhere to be tolerated, but rather in every place are to be utterly exterminated, as God, creator of all, so commands: “You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.” Of sorceresses, some summon demons by spells, others entice them by prayers and sacrifices, the rest by unspeakable things and ceremonies

To Maximilian Caesar 51

Summoning them, they draw them into the assistance of their own impiety. It is therefore not to be wondered at that witches seem to command demons, to whom they have become similar through the impiety of a perverse will, and, by mutual association, are united for the harm of the human race.

The second kind of wicked men who wish to command demons is that of those whom we commonly call necromancers. They profess arts full of execrations, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them openly visible, enclosed in crystal or some other vessel. These most pernicious men, full of falsehood and superstitions, commit evils so great that no good man could think them up.

For, in order to entice demons into service to themselves, they generally use most shameful sacrifices and enter into an express pact with them. They circulate many and various little books, full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, and deceitfully inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and wise men; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious persons, and draw them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise things great and altogether incredible, and by the hearing of these they falsely hold men suspended in wonder.

They say that by rings, pendants, images, exorcisms, and conjurations they can constrain malignant demons so that they appear visibly in a circle or in crystal, or in some vessel, and answer distinctly to all questions asked. All of them indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found to whom malignant spirits, even for evil purposes, are obedient in this way, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it, lest the curiosity of men, prone to novelties, con-

Demons obey, but only those with whom they are allied by pacts and acts of service; and when invoked by those whom they cannot otherwise keep faithful, they gladly come, although they falsely claim that they are compelled. It is therefore no wonder, most excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to obey depraved and perverse men, whom, as we have said, both likeness in malice and the destruction of the human race has made to be in agreement. But far be it from every Christian to wish, through a depraved likeness of will, to command demons. For if anyone in this life has begun to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the future he will burn with them without end.

But why good and righteous men cannot command the holy angels of God, though they have passed into their likeness of good will, I think the solution of this question would easily be given from what has been said above, if the difference of intelligences is recalled to mind. For although in the Church of God there are many men established whose righteousness benefits many unto salvation, yet in our times very few make such progress that, by reason of the merit of holiness, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it comes about that men of our age neither command malignant spirits by merit of holiness nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of holiness by which, working miracles in the Church, they have advanced as the saints once did, then they can both powerfully command demons and have the familiar fellowship of blessed spirits. For it is certain that holy men beloved by God in the primitive Church of the Christians once provided greater benefits to mortals through the cooperation of good spirits than

Sed quoniam omnis homo, in quantum creatura est, à Deo dependet, nihil potest agere si- ne illius voluntate, â quo velle habet posse. Quicquid igitur maleficae faciunt Deo sic permit- tente, sine cuius voluntate nihil possint, quia vt possint quod volunt, nisi Deus concesserit, neque â se, neque á daemonibus consequerentur, omnis itaque potestas à Domino Deo est, in quo ônia sut mo- uentur sicut in prima rerum omniu caufa, quoniam â quo libertatem arbitrij accepimus, ab ipso etiam posse quod volumus habemus, sed cum malefica- rum fit multum confusus intellectus, non arte hu- mana perpetrant mala quae faciunt, sed cooperatio- nedaemonum, quos vt natura subtiles, ita expe- rientia longa fecit ad producendum miranda velo- ces. Non enim causantur mirandi effectus malefi- carum ab huiufmodi medijs, quibus vtuntur ad ma- leficandum. Vt funt capita mortuorum, bufones, serpentes, characteres, imagines, his fimilia. To Emperor Maximilian.

... which the wickedness of depraved men, through the ministry of demons, could ever have brought upon [unclear]. For every true worshipper of God, if he has become like the holy angels, can do many wondrous things by prayers.

On the Power of Witches.

Sixth Question

Your invincible Majesty’s sixth question was: whence comes this so great power in witches, by which they are able to perpetrate so many, various, and wondrous things, even in a single hour, of such a kind and magnitude as none of the good could accomplish in his whole life?

If we wish to answer this question briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the holy Gospel, “Without me you can do nothing”; hence it is manifest that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God, and from nowhere else, whether men do good or evil. Hence the most holy prelate Augustine says: the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing is done visibly in this most ample and immense commonwealth of the whole creation which is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. Hence, Caesar, it must not be doubted that that power of the witches, in which, with the cooperation of demons, they produce wondrous and horrible effects, is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a man cannot even move his hand.

For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a human being or a beast of burden, unless almighty God wills it, consents to it, and grants the power that they may do what they have already resolved upon with perverse will. Unless God consents and wills, no creature can do anything; otherwise, if anything could be done without his willing and consenting, it would necessarily follow that God is weak, since he could not prevent what, against his will, he would be forced to permit to be done. But since every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both willing and being able.

Whatever, therefore, witches do, God permitting it thus, without whose will they could do nothing, since, unless God granted it, they would obtain neither from themselves nor from demons the ability to do what they wish: therefore all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved as in the first cause of all things, since from the one from whom we have received freedom of will, from him also we have the ability to do what we will. But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they perpetrate the evils they do not by human art, but by the cooperation of demons, whom, just as nature has made subtle, so long experience has made swift in producing wonders. For the wondrous effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things similar to these, but by the Devil who instituted these signs; since he is most proud, he desires in all things to be seen as comparable to God. For truly, just as almighty God instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which [unclear] worthily [unclear] signify [unclear] perpetrating [unclear] he seeks [unclear], which [unclear] as [unclear] with these [unclear] assists, he says it is evil. To Maximilian Caesar.

... for those who minister worthily, with him assisting, they signify and produce a saving effect, he who instituted them working salvation. Thus the devil, who desires nothing more than to be thought equal to God, has instituted certain signs as if they were sacraments; when he is invoked by those with whom he has entered into covenants by pacts, the malignant agent assists and, as often as God has permitted it, brings about the evil that is asked; if he has not permitted it, he does absolutely nothing. For the devil is the agent of all the necromantic effects of witches; by applying the means that he himself first instituted, he produces the desired work upon the subject matter, sometimes in reality, sometimes only in appearance.

But women witches, who, with their will now depraved, have passed by consent into the fellowship of demons through pacts, receive from them certain symbolic marks; when summoned by these, the demons immediately appear. In these pernicious operations of demons nothing is stronger than the foolish credulity of witches, which is increased by pacts and vows; when this has preoccupied the mind, the more firmly they have put faith at once in the demons’ signs, the more swiftly, with those demons cooperating, they obtain the operation. For the excessively savage depravity of the witches’ will in a certain way transforms them into [unclear], and when the mind permits this, they serve those who are raving. Plato related something similar in the book On the Poetic, saying: just as bacchant women, with unsound mind, are not able to draw [unclear]. Their spirit, carried outside itself into the fellowship of an evil demon, brings this about.

We have ascertained that witches, in times of swollen rivers, have drawn out butter, which can in no way happen otherwise than by the ministry of a demon. In like manner, when they have been brought into hatred of some man or beast and desire his destruction, they are driven by the gravest fury, thinking of nothing in their mind except vengeance. They take things familiar to them, known for witchcraft; they invoke demons; they show the signs instituted by them, together with characters; what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they achieve by the ministry of those demons.

But another person, who is not subjected to demons by a pact of surrender, even if he knows the things suitable for witchcraft and likewise the manner of working, although he displays the signs, rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the familiars of the demons. For the devil is so lifted up with pride that he emulates the Church of Christ: just as one who has not been ordained cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may utter the words of consecration, so also the demon, however much signs or characters are shown to him by one who invokes him, if he does not know that person to be subject to himself by pact, either never or rarely cooperates. For if he came everywhere to all who invoked him, without pacts having been interposed, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership.

Hence it is that many who are given over to profane arts, laboring with dreadful conjurations to summon demons to a circle, to a mirror, or to any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either the command of God stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious man not dedicated to him by homage. For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is clear that none is perpetrated: a witch raging in spirit and depraved in will; also the cooperation of a familiar devil; [unclear].

Et sicuti dae mones in potestate acumineque subtilitatis ab inui cem differunt, ita maleficarum potestas non est in omnibus vna, sed in singulis, pro vt daemonibus concurrunt natura subtilioribus vel grossioribus, diuersa. Multa enim sunt genera daemonum, &; cer tis inter se gradibus distant, ratione locorum, in quae cadentes à principio sunt detrusi. Primum quidem genus daemonum appellatur igneum, quod circa superiorem peruagatur aerem nec vnquam ante iudicij diem ad inferiora demer gitur, sed continuè sub regionibus permanentes lunaribus, nullum habent cum hominibus inter ra commertium. [unclear]: and, before all else, divine permission. But if one of these does not concur, the evil deed cannot be perpetrated. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not meet the wicked woman’s will, she would perpetrate no evil deed. Again, if the witch is lacking, the devil will in no way consummate the evil deed. For the devil uses the will of the raving witch, like a craftsman using an instrument for working, without which he cannot inflict the evil deed. And just as demons differ from one another in power and in keenness of subtlety, so the power of witches is not one and the same in all, but is diverse in each individual, according as demons of a subtler or grosser nature concur with them. For there are many kinds of demons, and they are separated from one another by fixed degrees, by reason of the places into which, when they fell at the beginning, they were thrust down.

The first kind of demons is called fiery; it wanders about the upper air and is never cast down to the lower regions before the day of judgment, but, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, has no intercourse on earth with human beings. That it remains beneath the moon, Saint Augustine bears witness in the work On the Christian Combat, saying thus: demons do not dwell in heaven, where the sun and stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region. Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, because Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals, furnished with little wings, have rather often been seen flying about; they spend their whole life in fire, since they are born with fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to the place from which they had come. They have no associations with witches, because, since they dwell in fire, on account of their subtlety they cannot put on a gross or aerial body.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

The second kind is called aerial, which, wandering in the air, dwells near us. Indeed they can descend to the lower regions and, having assumed bodies from the thicker air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. With God permitting, they quite often disturb the air, stir up thunder and storms; all together they conspire for the destruction of the human race. They are moved, in the manner of human beings, by the affections of the passions; they are touched especially by pride and envy and by continual disturbances. They are not clothed with a solid body, nor do they remain in one place, nor do they all have one form, but many, and they change these rather often according to the variety of the affections by which, either summoned by the incantations of witches, they come to meet them, or, driven by disturbance, they move to do harm. For they have an altogether violent, frenzied character, full of disturbances; hence, when greatly agitated by evil-working, they very often devise sudden ambushes. While making their attacks, they partly wish to lie hidden, partly they inflict violence. Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are so much the more powerful for evil-working, the higher in that order the one who assists them is whom they have obtained. In the life of Saint Anthony, Saint Athanasius said that the air is full of demons, which Mercury, thrice-greatest, had said before: namely, that no part of the world is devoid of the presence of demons. The holy prelate Ambrose also says: the world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickednesses. Hence the Platonists [say that] demons flying in the air in the manner of a very dense

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] of fiery snow have been handed down as visible to those who desire them, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they have continued their gazes toward the sky with eyes not struck back; but I do not know whether the object is produced in the air from a real consistency, or whether the interrupted motion of the eyes represents false images, not without harm to the sense. Yet I have made a slight experiment of the things mentioned above.

The third kind, however, we call terrestrial demons, whom we do not at all doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth for their deserts. Concerning these the most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, Theophorus, once Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: “Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and terrestrial spirits alike is made void.” Of these demons, some dwell in woods and groves, and lay snares for hunters. Others live in open fields, and make travelers wander at night; some abide in hidden places and caves; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight to dwell with human beings in darkness. They are not led by one disposition but by a varied one, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Of these, some rejoice in terrifying human beings by illusions alone; others desire, by predictions of future events, to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves. Some, however, labor with the greatest effort to this end: that they may terrify, harm, or kill people disturbed by irrational madness or raging with melancholy, which we have recognized by experience to have happened rather often. Hence Saint John Chrysostom, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: “More powerful than every diabolical action for doing no harm is the greatness of sorrow, because the demon overcomes whomever he overcomes through sorrow; if you take this away, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon.” This kind of demons, however, is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy and lightness of its affections, whereby they rejoice in terrifying many rather than in being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet they sometimes dwell with, or make promises to, mad women, in glass or in crystal or in a mirror; and when stirred up by incantations they give replies to women, and if someone who is to come has cursed them on the road, they announce it beforehand. And this kind of witches differs in some respects greatly from the rest, since what the former make sick by witchcraft, these promise to cure. But because for the most part they repel witchcraft by witchcraft, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, since, immersing itself in liquids, it dwells about lakes and rivers, full of anger, disturbed, restless, and deceitful. In the sea it stirs up storms, and, sinking ships into the deep, takes life from many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, they more often appear in the female sex, and are more rarely seen in the male, because they live in damp places and follow a softer course of life; nor can they easily assume a base form by the custom of the others. Hence antiquity long ago named the Naiads and Nereids, nymphs of the waters, not in the male but in the female sex. By our people, however, they are called by the common term aquatic women, that is, Wasser Frawen. Those, however, who dwell in drier and rather arid places, whenever they appear bodily visible to human beings, transform themselves into men.

TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. xerunt, stupenda mirātibus ostendentes spectacula, &amp; quasi beatorum ibi sint mansiones amicos se vi- uorum mentiuntur. Et hoc genus daenonum cum maleficis mu- lieribus nullum consueuit habere commertium. Sextum verò daenonum genus appellatur luci- fugum, propterea quod lucem maximè horrent et amp; detestantur, quia nec diebus vnquam apparent, nec alio modo corpus, quam de nocte possunt as- sumere. Hoc est negocium quod in tenebris per- ambulat, genus daenonum imperscrutabile ac pe- nitus tenebrosum, passionibusque frigidis agitatum; maliciosum, inquietum et amp; perturbatum, quod oc- currentes homines nocturnis violenter comprimit horis, saepiusque (Deo permittente) aut flatu quos- dam interficit aut contactu. Maleficis non conuenit hoc genus daemonū neque carminibus actari potest, quia lucem fugit et amp; voces hominum, simulque omnē tumultū aëreum maximè ad maleficia feminārū cō- sueuit occurrere quoniā caeteris omnibus est magis subtile et amp; audacissimae temeritatis. Terrestrium quoque nonnulli maleficis vt est dictum subseruiunt, qui tamen inferiori gradu habiti maiora illa male- ficia inducere minimè possunt. Constat igitur ma- nifestè, quod tota potestas maleficarum, in qua tam̄ miranda faciunt, daenonibus â Domino Deo limitata conceditur, &amp; quando ille nōpermittit, nihil operantur. DE PER-

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] they also assume forms of beasts, according as they are touched by various emotions. But the holy angels, since they are never altered by emotion, always appear uniformly in male form. For nowhere do we read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast whatsoever, but always in male appearance. Yet demons have often been seen around rivers and springs in the appearance of women, sometimes dancing, sometimes letting down their hair in the manner of women, and sometimes indeed speaking with human beings and practicing various deceptions. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have dealings with witches.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. And these demons are the worst in disposition, and they especially attack those who dig wells and mines and who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make chasms in the earth, and [unclear] flame-spewing winds; suddenly they vanish at a sign and return to their hiding places. At times the sound of little bells is heard among them, and they sometimes falsely claim that they are spirits of men deceased from life. They seek nothing more than the fear and wonder of human beings. Hence we have found by experience that they sometimes led certain of the simpler sort of men into their mountain hiding places.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

They led them, showing astonishing spectacles to those who marveled, and they falsely claim to be friends of the living, as if the dwellings of the blessed were there. Among these demons also some are incubones of treasures which the avarice of mortals has hidden in the earth; and lest they come again into the use of men, they withdraw them, steal them, guard them, and sometimes transport them from place to place. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have any dealings with female witches.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they especially dread and detest the light, since they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any way except by night. This is the business that walks about in darkness, an unsearchable and utterly dark kind of demon, agitated by cold passions; malicious, restless, and disturbed, which violently presses upon people it meets in the hours of night, and more often, God permitting, kills certain persons either by breath or by touch. This kind is not suited to witches, nor can it be driven by incantations, because it flees light and the voices of human beings, and at the same time every disturbance of the air. It is especially accustomed to attend upon the witchcraft of women, since it is more subtle than all the rest and of the most audacious rashness. Some of the terrestrial demons also, as has been said, serve witches, who nevertheless, being held in a lower rank, are by no means able to bring about those greater acts of witchcraft. It is therefore plainly evident that the whole power of witches, by which they do such wondrous things, is granted to demons under limitation by the Lord God; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

To Maxim. Caesar.
