On Divine Permission

Seventh Question

The seventh question of Your Most Serene Majesty was this: why almighty God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permits such great misdeeds to be done to the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocent persons perish, grievously tortured.

To this question, when I was formerly placed before your majesty, I remember that I answered as follows. Almighty God, just, upright, kindly, merciful, whatever he permits, permits justly, because he is just; there is no iniquity with him, but in true judgment he either does or permits all things that are done. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, we answer: he permits them because he is just.

Let not the answer we have given seem absurd to Your Majesty, O Caesar, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For indeed, if he did not permit evils to be done, then man could not sin; he would certainly be impeccable, which does not befit his nature, to which from the beginning the creator of all things gave free will. For since man is a creature and not the creator, he is necessarily as capable of being turned to good as to evil; his being depends upon the supreme maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends upon the cause of its being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and eternal; everything corruptible necessarily fails, but it is preserved by the goodness of the creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor ought to have happened that man, by the condition of his nature, should be created impeccable; naturally this is enjoyed by God alone, the maker of all things, who is immutable and eternal.

But whenever it is granted to man that he seems unable to sin, neither is the freedom of will taken away, nor is the possibility simply removed, but the will is confirmed in good. And whenever this gift is conferred on a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning; he left him in the hand of his own counsel. For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should have free will and yet be unable to commit sin. For most holy Augustine says: the first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last freedom in glory will be much more [unclear], he would not have dominion over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, he nevertheless justly permits men to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of will remains, the virtue of a good work may receive its merit, and voluntary depravity may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits men to sin and to do evil, to whom from the beginning he granted freedom of will. But there are many reasons long since assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great crimes to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall briefly make mention in order as necessary.

The first is so that the excellence of the divine power may be manifested, since he alone is immutable above every [unclear].

Permi- fit autem homini Deus voluntatem liberam, cui nec reges imperant nec principes. [unclear]. But every mutable creature has no comparison with the immutable Creator. Hence in Numbers it is read: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should be changed. In Isaiah too it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit also it is written: Just are you, O Lord; all your judgments are true; all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty; for he will render to a man his work, and will repay each according to his ways. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness openly recognizes how he is nothing when compared with his Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, so that, since the freedom of choice is preserved, the excellence of the great God may become known to men.

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, which knows how to draw good from our evils, when it makes one person’s sin become another’s merit, for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, which of us would understand the good? For the good of God orders; but evils he does not do, but, when they have been done by the impious, he himself disposes them so that they may not come about in disorder. Nor does the malice of men hinder the will of God, nor can man do anything which God does not permit.

The third cause is that the Almighty permits wicked deeds to be done in order to manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and have done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, neither could God be merciful; but since in many things we all offend, everywhere God finds something to forgive, everywhere a guilty person presents himself, in whom the pious Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised and would not be sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not be ended. Therefore where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, gathers together into one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason of divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance, since if all did good and no one sinned, the justice of God would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have a place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will render to each according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse than the beasts, which, with no violence impelling them, freely use the motions of nature. For even if brute animals lack reason, nevertheless they have the free motion of nature, which they follow; in comparison with them man would seem of an inferior condition if he did not have the free choice of the will. But God permitted man a free will, over which neither kings nor princes rule.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of constancy in human virtue, since we praise a just man for this reason: that, although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God helping him, remained in the constancy of a good will.

[unclear] demons to perform such great evil deeds through the intervention of witches, is so that those who, having despised the truth, delight in falsehood may, seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood, be utterly deceived. For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who disdain to follow the saving teachings of Christ, deceived by demons, should all be plunged down to hell to be punished forever: they seek help from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have worshiped. For it is just that he who, abandoning the truth of his own free will, clings to falsehood should be cast headlong by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose mighty virtue is above every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits the devil great things and denies him certain small things, he makes manifest how weak the enemy of the human race is, subject in all things to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing of himself, but everything that he does, he does by God’s permission. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God has permitted acts of witchcraft to be done, is justice, by which he preserves in inviolable order the freedom that he once bestowed upon the creature from the beginning. But since the power of every creature dependent on its creator is restricted and limited, it is clear that neither can the devil do everything he wills, nor can man, however depraved in will. The will indeed is free, but power is limited by certain necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wish, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would overthrow everything. The bound power of demons, however, the history of holy Job clearly demonstrates by example:

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

Satan did not dare to tempt him further than had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if they could always use a free power to harm according to their own judgment. Before the Lord’s passion, however, they used a greater freedom of power than afterward. But when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power was thereafter greatly diminished, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of the world will be cast out.” For the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints greatly restrained the audacity of demons, so that they can rightly be called instigators of evils, but by no means drivers. Nor would the Devil prevail against us unless he received strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you”; again, “Do not give place to the devil.” Therefore, in concluding the discourse for the understanding of the proposed question, why God permits so many acts of witchcraft to be done, I believe the reasons have been sufficiently made clear. For although the will of demons is always wicked, nevertheless their power can never be unjust, since what they wickedly will they have from their own choice, but what they can do wickedly they have only from God. And these things have been said as far as concerns those who do evil.

But why does almighty God permit demons to injure, through the agency of witches, human beings who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? Qui vero maleficos non accedit propter ea, quoniam Deus prohibuit, malens vivere cum obferuantiis mandatorum Dei in aegestate et aegritudine, quam contra Deum in diuitiis et corporis fanitate, ille Deum veraciter diligit et integritatem fidei Christianae reet cultidit. To Maximilian Caesar.

...of [unclear] and of the faithful, the judgment of permission would rightly seem to be just. But now, more often, the good and innocent are weakened by the harmful arts of demons, and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods which those bewitched often suffer. It troubles many why the Almighty permits these things, he who permits nothing unjustly.

For this proposed question, I shall set forth in order, as briefly as I can, the necessary reasons, no other than those I have received from the ancient and Catholic doctors.

And the first reason is the testing of the faith of Christians and the experience of their integrity: that, scourged by the harmful arts of demons, they may learn, in the sufferings of the flesh, what faith and love toward God they possess in the hidden place of the mind. In prosperity it is not difficult to be long-suffering; but in adversity, to await help from the savior of the faithful with humble patience belongs not to the soft, but to the strong and truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith toward God he had, who before, in tranquillity, had preserved piety without the dart of temptation. Hence it must also be noted that those whom the harmful arts of demons or men have in any way made ill, who, in order to recover health, either approach or consult any sorcerers and enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the precepts of God and of the Church, and have neither true faith in God nor love, seeking health not from Christ but from the devil and his minister. For they prefer to live healthy, but unhappily, in the name of the devil, rather than to suffer a little here for the love of Christ and afterward to rejoice with him forever.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

But he who does not approach sorcerers on these grounds, because God has forbidden it, preferring to live, with observance of God's commandments, in poverty and sickness rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith. Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, men corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith are not to be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by harmful arts, who reveal thefts and adulteries by the ministry of demons, who foretell future things by inspection of stones or mirrors. Do not hear them, I pray, who, ignorant of divine law, would wish ministers of demons of this sort to exist under your command, because they know how to undo spells by spells; for such pernicious treatment of bodies brings about the death of souls, and makes men withdraw from God, the creator of all things, and adhere to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

Secondly, the reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be injured by witchcraft is the increase of merits, namely that their patience, proved in tribulation, may deserve a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says: man is unknown to himself, as to what he can bear and what he cannot; sometimes he thought he could not bear what nevertheless he can. When temptation comes, as if some interrogator, a man is found by himself, who before, lying hidden, did not know himself. The divine chief apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others, how inconsiderate and weak he was; he received it, and the weakness that lay hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest testing of man, as sacred Scripture bears witness,

Quo contra de malis et reprobis ita scriptũ legimus: quare impij viuunt, subleuati sunt con- fortatique diuitiis domus eorum securae sunt et paca- catae, & non est virga Dei super illos, ducunt in bo- nis dies suos, & in puncto ad inferna descendunt. Manifestum enim damnationis est signum, si hic ma- le viuas in peccatis et vitiis, Deo contrarius et in bonis fortunae corporisque sanitate prosperatus. Quinta ratio quod omnipotens permittit ho- mines bonos et iustos tribulari â malis et reprobis, est propter mentis omnimodã purgationem. Nam sicut scriptura dicit, nõ est homo iustus in terra qui faciat bonum et non peccet, sed cum Deus nullùm peccatum transeat impunitũ, ordinat iustus homi- nibus per misericordiam pro eorum delictis poenas temporales, impiis verò et reprobis per iusticiã ae- ternas.

To Emperor Maximilian.

The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men. Patience is easy in prosperity, when no adversity strikes the mind. But many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the guarding of humility, so that the faithful and righteous man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and with men they shall not be scourged.” Therefore pride held them; they were covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity comes forth as though from fat. It belongs to God’s mercy that he sometimes permits good and righteous men to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagining of evildoers makes the good man fear his God and diligently invoke his help, strengthened by which he may trust that he is safe against the assaults of demons. But let no proud man, presuming on his own powers, think himself safe from the harmful arts of demons, since the man whom, swollen with pride, God’s protection abandons, without doubt lies open to the harmful arts of demons.

The fourth reason is that there may be a distinction between the good and the wicked. For Scripture says of good men, beloved by God, in the Acts of the Apostles, that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. And Saint Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.” The most wise King Solomon also says in Proverbs: “The Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and as a father in the son [unclear].”

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

he is pleased with him. It is a matter too glorious for a Christian patiently to endure adversities for the love of God, whether they are brought on by wicked men or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and righteous men, not for their confusion, as the petitioners suppose, but rather for the greatest and sure consolation of the soul. Indeed, when a righteous man lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeping his commandments with all care, and nevertheless is troubled by evildoers, whether in body or in possessions or in both, that man is truly blessed, because when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the Catholic faith of Christians and patiently endures the evils he receives in this world for the love of God has a sure sign that he has persevered in the grace of God to be saved. On the contrary, we read this written of the wicked and reprobate: “Why do the impious live, exalted and strengthened by riches? Their houses are secure and at peace, and the rod of God is not upon them; they pass their days in good things, and in a moment descend to hell.” For it is a manifest sign of damnation if here you live wickedly in sins and vices, opposed to God, and prospered in the goods of fortune and the health of the body.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and righteous men to be troubled by the wicked and reprobate is for the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says, there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin; but since God lets no sin pass unpunished, through mercy he ordains temporal punishments for righteous men for their offenses, but through justice eternal punishments for the impious and reprobate.

To Emperor Maximilian.

[unclear]. Therefore, out of mercy, he changes for the penitent eternal punishment into temporal punishment, which they must necessarily suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and most grievous, merciful God is accustomed to purge in this life, in various ways, the penitents whom he loves, through the hardships of diverse tribulations in body and in possessions. For the malice of the impious benefits good and just men as a remedy, but for those who inflict it, it leads to damnation.

The sixth reason is that a man bewitched through the assaults of demons may be called back to repentance and may set in his heart the necessary amendment of life. For almighty God does not immediately send vengeance when we sin, but awaits our amendment until the appointed time. But if we neglect to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; we sinners who have disdained to acknowledge him by repenting in tranquillity shall at last acknowledge him, late, in tribulation. Hence the holy Prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they do not keep my commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I shall not scatter from them, nor shall I do harm in my truth.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the witchcrafts of demons to prevail against good and innocent persons is so that an excessively licentious occasion for sinning may be cut off from them. For there are many poor, sick, good, devout, humble persons pleasing to God, whom poverty and bodily illness preserve in the love of God, and who, if they were rich and raised to honors, would quickly fall away from the purpose of holiness into the abyss of vices. It is not beneficial for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, the just, and the innocent to be subject to various calamities; sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil men, sometimes in diverse other ways and by other means, he takes away from such persons riches and honors, which he foreknew they would use badly, so that they may keep humility in poverty and abasement, which they would certainly not have preserved if placed in wealth and exaltation. He also often permits them to fall into many great illnesses, for whom glad health of the flesh would have brought the greatest sickness of mind.

Finally, he permits certain persons to be driven to death by witchcraft, so that the license for sinning may be cut off from them, which they would have abused had they been allowed to remain longer in life. Hence Scripture says of the just man: He was snatched away, lest malice change his understanding, or deceit deceive his soul.

The eighth reason for divine permission is so that men may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have great power against all witchcrafts of malignant spirits. For one who venerates with due honor the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church is rarely harmed by the witchcrafts of demons. And especially the hearing of witches and the use of things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. For they are not blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be feared by demons as signs that display the protection of divine defense. But concerning infant children

To Maximilian Caesar.

As for infants who, reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the evil arts of demons or of men, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by evil arts because of the sins of their parents.

On the Providence of God. Question Eight.

This was the eighth question of Your Serenity: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as also by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a certain and infallible providence over all and each of those things which are done in the world.

I remember that I answered this question as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence, by whose will and command they were brought forth into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion first, indeed, from the Scriptures, and afterward by arguments, as briefly as may be allowed. In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise King Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth so as to cause your soul to sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered against your words, scatter all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies to providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and one of them does not fall upon the earth before God?” A great commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for men, but also for tiny birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little later he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?”

Almighty God, because he created all things and brought them forth into being when they did not exist, rules and governs the universe, lest it slip away and flow into dissolution. This could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it is necessary that the ordered continuity of the whole universe be thrown into confusion. But the providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds and gives their food to the beasts of burden, and fills every living creature with blessing, and clothes the grass of the fields, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful comeliness, cannot forget man, whom he created from the beginning in his own image. He cares for all things, who governs all things; and he bears providence not only for man, but also for all beasts of burden, in whose dominion all things are placed, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us now, therefore, consider this immense structure of the whole universe, how in its original arrangement and motion it always persists, ordered in the highest degree, and how that divine and unchangeable providence, unless we stray shamefully in mind, preserves, directs, and governs these things by the clearest reason [unclear].

To Maximilian Caesar 79

[unclear] we shall understand: Then let us contemplate all earthly things, how in the most orderly fashion each and every thing is born and proceeds in its natural disposition; this cannot happen by chance, but they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created. Next, indeed, the earth placed in the middle of the world, like a point or center that unfolds the circle, equally distant from the whole universe: nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing, finally, more delightful to the sense could have offered itself for contemplation.

In this point of an immense mass, enclosed wondrously by that very mass, we see all things ordered, and that nothing can be left unordered, so that we may know for certain that all things which at times seem to us somehow to drift are subject to order: by the simple and wholly unchangeable nod, the whole structure of the entire universe, assembled from so many diverse and movable things, conspires and is governed in the most orderly way. Certainly we see, in those things that present themselves to our sense, that the greater the intelligence and power that arises with time in any governor, the less can anything unordered happen there by chance. Since, therefore, that supreme intellect, creator of all things, preserver and ruler, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, surely no place is ever left to rash chance, which might hinder the will of so great a majesty.

Therefore the whole of what is anywhere, or can be, is comprehended under the command of one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. To us, however, unexpected events occur, because we are changeable and are changed almost daily, having no determinate knowledge of future things.

John Trithemius, Eight Questions 80

But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, understands all things together and at once: his providence is not deceived; his will is never varied; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never intercepted, even if at times his sentence seems to be changed. Hence, if we attend carefully, we plainly understand that the ends of things and of motions will declare that all these lower things are made, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence; from its command nothing at all is alien.

For God himself, ruler of all things, understands both all things and individual things, not dispersed into many things after our manner, but abiding in himself as one indivisible thing; by gazing upon himself as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes, and through causes beholding the cause of all things, he cares for all things by beholding them, and provides for individual things, directing them to a good end by an eternal order. Come now, most wise Caesar, so that we may understand divine providence, governing all things, let us use reasons, as briefly as we can, for a more attentive [unclear]. And so, if God's action is his own proper intelligence, which no wise man fails to admit, as at once most eminent and most inward, as much as he acts, just so much does he understand, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but also in the smallest. Therefore he understands individual things. Indeed, from the first Being, through individual things that are beings in whatever way, following in fixed orders, there is the most ample influence; and those things which act after him are everywhere moved and act by his power.

Either, therefore, God understands or acts nothing outside himself, which is false; or, by acting, he also understands all things and individual things.

AD MAXIM. CAESAREM. 71 tiam eadem intelligit, quod est verum. Nusquam enim fieret, nisi prius (vt more nostro loquamur) intelligerentur ab ipso Deo qui facit ea, sicuti non fiunt à sole, quae non prospiciuntur ab eo. Verum quia omnia singula quae facit omnipotens intel- ligit, haud dubium quin disponit, regit ordinat omnia quae fecit, â quo res non solum habent vt sint sed etiam vt causae quaedam aliarum rerum. Itaque si habent à Deo res vt sint causae, inde quoque accepe- runt, officium causae proprium, hoc est conseruare pro viribus curare quod fecerunt. Quocirca si á prima causa omnes causae hanc habent proprieta- tem, in quantum sunt quaedam causae merito ipsa hanc bonitatem naturaliter habet a prouidentiam, vt omnia curet, singula quae fecit, in quantum maximè causa eost eorum omnium singulorum. Quae quidem nisi singillatim custodiantur ab eo qui facit ea, non custodientur vnquam communia quae conseruantur in singulis. Nec enim conséruabitur totum, quod ex partibus constat si partes ipsae negli- gantur. Ex intentione igitur intelligentiae primae maximaque communis prouenit vniuersalis distin- ctio rerum. Ipsa verò per se distinguitur ab alijs, ceteraque inter se suae notionis norma distinguit.Vn- de sicut distinctissime Deus omnia singula nouit, ita distinctissime regit, moderatur curat.Mani- festum igitur puto clementissime Cęsar Maximilia- ne satis ostensum, quod prouidentia summi re- ctoris Dei inferiora omnia singula amplectitur, disponit, regit moderatur, alioquin sine obser- uantis prouida dispositione hunc ordinem quem cernimus pulcherrimum nullatenus continuarent. Nec me fugit quam variè quondam huius mundi F sapiens- 72 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. sapientes de prouidentia fuerint opinati. Ex his quidam non prouidentia sed casu factum hunc mundum arbitrati sunt, quorum si esset opinio ve- ra, multis relinqueretur prouidentiae locus, sed ne- cessariò fluitarent omnia,cum eo mundus quo fa- ctus est casu posset interire. Iterumque dixit: omnium generatio rerum cunctusque mutabilium naturarum progres- sus.Et quicquid mouetur aliquando causas, ordi- nem, formas ex diuinae mentis stabilitate fortitur. Alij verò Deû incorruptibilia duntaxat curare putabant, vt sunt caelestia substantiae separata, si- mul species rerum,caetera verò cuncta nescire penitusque negligere.Sed hi turpiter errauerunt, quoniam omnipotens non solum vniuersalium incorruptibilium , sed etiam particularium corruptibilium prouidentiam habet cu- ram.Vnde sanctus iterum Bôetius dicit:Sedet in terra conditor altus, rerumque regens flectit ha- benas,Rex dominus fons origo lex sapiens arbiter aequi. Alijverò neglectum se iri non ferentes,homi- nem propter intellectus praeeminentiã de numero corruptibilia exemerunt dicentes, Deum homi- nes curam prouidentiam habere,reliqua verò terre-

To Emperor Maximilian.

also understands those same things, which is true. For nothing would ever come to be unless first, to speak in our customary way, it were understood by God himself, who makes these things, just as things are not made by the sun which are not looked upon by it. But because the Almighty understands each and every thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made; from him things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from him also they have received the proper office of a cause, that is, according to their powers to preserve and care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, rightly does that first cause naturally have this goodness and providence, so that it cares for all things, each thing that it has made, insofar as it is especially the cause of all and each of them. Indeed, unless these are guarded individually by him who makes them, the common things which are preserved in individuals will never be guarded. For the whole, which consists of parts, will not be preserved if the parts themselves are neglected. Therefore from the intention of the first and greatest common intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things. But it is distinguished of itself from others, and distinguishes the rest among themselves by the rule of its knowledge. Hence, just as God knows each and every thing most distinctly, so he most distinctly rules, moderates, and cares for them. Therefore, most clement Emperor Maximilian, I think it is clear and sufficiently shown that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and moderates all lower things, each and every one; otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who watches over them, they would in no way continue this most beautiful order which we perceive. Nor does it escape me how variously the wise men of this world once held opinions about providence.

The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius.

Of these, some thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance. If their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift uncertainly, since the world could perish by the same chance by which it was made.

Against their false opinion others taught that the world could neither have been made without reason, nor certainly stand unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by eternal reason, begetter of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity, and, remaining unmoved, grant that all things be moved.” And again he said: “The generation of all things and the whole progress of mutable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, receive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.”

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as heavenly things, separated substances, and likewise the species of things, but that he did not know all the rest and utterly neglected them. But these men erred shamefully, since the Almighty has providence and care not only for incorruptible universals, but also for corruptible particulars. Hence holy Boethius again says: “Meanwhile the high creator sits, and ruling all things bends the reins: king, lord, source, origin, law, wise arbiter of justice. This is the common love of all things, and they seek to be held by the end of the good, because they cannot otherwise endure, unless, by love turned back again, they flow back to the cause that gave them being.”

Others, however, unable to bear that they themselves would be neglected, exempted man, because of the preeminence of his intellect, from the number of corruptible things, saying that God has care and providence for human beings, but the rest of earthly

45
AD MAXIM. CAESAREM. 73 terrestria cuncta despicere. Contra quorum falsam opinionem et satis reor dictum, & multa produce- re omnino superfluum. Ait enim scriptura: homi- nes et iumenta saluabis domine: Et in alio loco quidam sapiens dixit: pusillum et magnum fecit dominus et aequaliter est illi cura de omnibus. Om- nia igitur et singula inferiora, magna et parua, cor- ruptibilia et incorruptibilia diuinae maiestatis pro- uidentia ordinat, regit, disponit et curat, cuius vo- luntas potentissima ex nihilo omnia producit, sa- cra iterum protestante scriptura: Tua verò pater prouidentia ab initio cuncta gubernat. Erubescant igitur homines mente corrupti et impij ac reprobi, circa fidem Christianam, qui vana loquacitate in- flatî prouidentiam omnia scientis auferunt, & quantam Deo iniuriam faciant non attendunt. Quid enim vt Firmiani vt amur sententia, tam di- gnum, tamque proprium omnipotenti Deo, quam prouidentia? Sed si nihil prouidet, si inferiora ne- gligit, si mortalia non curat, amisit iam omnem di- gnitatem. Sed impossibile est, sancto attestante Anshelmo, Deum honoremsuum perdere, quoni- am, sicut peripateticus ait, in aeternis non est ma- lum, nec corruptio, nec peccatum. Qui ergò pro- uidentiam tollit, totam Dei substantiam tollit, & quid dicit nisi Deum non esse. Sed dicant mihi nunc, qui Dei prouidentiam negant inferiora curare. Si Deus inferiora negligit, attentant, quid necessariò sequatur. Si Deus scien- ter nos negligit et contemnit, non est iam deinceps causa qua ipsũ vel cultu profequamur, vel religio- ne veneremur beneficiũ, quin potius neglecti et cõ- tempti negligamus et illũ ipsi. Si verò nesciens no- F 2 contem- 74 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. contemnit ac negligit, penitus iam causa non est, vt nescientem nos et ob id nihil boni con- ferre potentem, colamus aut praecibus inuo- cemus. Nam si non curat humana Deus siue sci- ens, siue nesciens, cessat oninsis causa pietatis, cum fit spes nulla salutis. Quae nam potest inter morta- les pietatis esse consideratio, quae spes animarum sa- luris, si Deus humana non curat? Enimuero si pro- uidentia tollitur, quem colimus, quem adoramus? si non est apud Deum prouidentia mortalium, certè neque beneficia praestat hominibus neque poenas de- sertoribus imponit, neque mortales iuuare potest nec vult, nec omnino curat, nec quid agamus ad- uertit, & neque praeces neque orationes cuiusquã ex- audit. Cur autem illi cultum exhibemus vllum, cur honorem, cur praeces, aut quare nescientem nos Deum tantopere metuimus vel timemus qui nobis neglectis atque contemptis, neque benefacere potest neque male? prouidentia enim sublata, neque sanctitas neque religio subsistet, quibus extinctis, perturbatio vitae sequetur maxima et confufio horrenda. Pieta- te in Deum sublata, quid iam erit respublica, nisi confusio sempiterna? peribit necessario fides ho- minum publica, societasque humani generis, iusticia- que omnis vna simul euanescent et peribunt. Quid erit de fide Christiara sentiendum, si Deus non cu- rat humana, quid Denique de saluatore omnium do- mino nostro Iesu Christo, nisi fabula inanis et ficti- tium totum reputabitur, si non est prouidentia Dei mortalia curans. Prouide quicquid in hac vita bo- ni agimus, quicquid pro Dei amore mali sustine- mus, vanum est totum ac nobis inutile, si ille de no- bis curam non habet vllam. Videant nunc et horreant, qui prouidentiam Dei

To Maximilian Caesar.

to despise all earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has been said, and to bring forward many more things would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “Men and beasts you will save, O Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has care equally for all.” Therefore the providence of the divine majesty orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all and each of the lower things, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; its most powerful will produces all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again declares: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.” Therefore let men corrupted in mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, blush: men who, puffed up with vain talkativeness, take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he foresees nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has already lost all dignity. But it is impossible, as holy Anselm attests, for God to lose his honor, since, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, nor corruption, nor sin. Therefore he who removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say except that God does not exist?

But now let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things tell me. If God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is thereafter no reason why we should pursue him with worship or venerate him with religious devotion as a benefactor; indeed rather, being neglected and despised, let us ourselves neglect him too. But if, not knowing, he despises and neglects us, there is now utterly no reason why we should worship one who does not know us and for that reason is unable to confer any good, or invoke him with prayers.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause of piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope of the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is removed, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, certainly he neither bestows benefits on human beings nor imposes punishments on deserters, nor can or will he help mortals, nor does he care at all, nor notice what we do, and he hears neither the entreaties nor the prayers of anyone. But why do we offer him any worship, why honor, why prayers, or why do we so greatly fear or dread a God who does not know us, who, with us neglected and despised, can do us neither good nor ill? For with providence removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and a dreadful confusion will follow. With piety toward God removed, what will the commonwealth then be, except everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings will necessarily perish, and the fellowship of the human race, and all justice will vanish and perish at once. What is to be thought of the Christian faith, if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, of the Savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, except that the whole will be regarded as an empty fable and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Surely whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us, if he has no care for us at all.

Let those now see and shudder who [unclear] the providence of God

DEI negant cum finem opinionis suae desperatio- nem omnium pessimam intueantur. Nemo igitur se vaniloquentia Philosophorum secularium in- ductus ad contemptũ Dei erudiat, nemo prouiden- tiam summi et incommutabilis boni tollat, nemo dignitatem creatoris omnium corrumpat. Omnes enim qui prouidentiam negant diuinam, beneficijs clementissimi Saluatoris et indignos le praestant et ingratos. Firmiter enim credendum est et nullatenus du- bitandum hunc modum vniuersum, tam visibilem quam inuisibilem, omniaque et singula, quae vel in célo sunt vel in terra et in mari, diuina prouidentia regi et gubernari, & nihil penitus in toto vniuerso ab eius cura alienum. Nam et fruges et reliqua om- nia, quae terra parit, tempestates quoque ac varietates temporũ caelique mutationes, quibus omnia, quę ter- ra gignit naturata pubescunt, diuina prouidentia generi humano praestat, procuratque omnia et singu- la, nec solum magna, sed et minima quaeque vsque a- deo vt nec tenuissimum quidem arboris folium in terram decidat sine voluntate omnipotentis Dei patris, qui creauit illud et regit et curat. Si quis au- tem putat hanc tantam totius vniuersi magnitudi- nem ab vno Deo qui solus est, non posse regi et gu- bernari, nimiū fallitur, & quanta sit virtus diuinae potestatis nescire comprobatur. Enim uero qui v- niuersum mundum ex nihilo potuit in esse produ- cere, etiam quod fecit prudentissimèin sempiternũ potest gubernare. Omnia enim nouit, omnia intelli- git, ônia potest, qui solus õnipotens omnia creauit. Nos igitur sancto Euangelio credentes diui- nam imprimis prouidentiam veneremur, mentes quoque nostras qua possum virtute sursum eriga- musab 76 IOA. TRITEMII OCTO QVAEST. mus ab his quae sunt caduca, & nobis ipsis redacti vniamur, quatenus Dei maiestatem vbique praesen- tem fideliter intelligamus, quae cum fit omninò in- circumscriptibilis, tenet omnia, implet omnia, complectitur omnia, superexcedit omnia et fusti- net omnia.Non autē ex vna parte sustinet atque ex a- lia superexcedit, neque ex vna parte implet, atque e x alia circumplectitur, sed circumplectendo implet et amp; implendo circumplectitur, sustinendo superex- cedit, superexcedendo sustinet omnia, qui per molem corporis nusquam est, per inscriptibilem substantiam suam nusquam deest, qui oculis carnis non cernitur, qui per fidem in cordis puritate vide- tur. O virtus inexplicabilis, ô pietas incompraehen- sibilis, ô sapientia ineffabilis, ô diuinitas incircum- scriptibilis, quae non partibus constas vt corpus, non affectibus distas vt anima, non formis substas vt caetera omnia quae per te facta sunt, qui es in omni- bus super omnia regens gubernās sapientissi- me vniuersa.His itaque testimonijs sacratissime Cae- far Maximiliane, satis vt reor, probatum est, mun- dum hunc vniuersum Dei prouidentia gubernari, qui cum fit intellectus purus, simplex increatus et sempiternus omnia nouit, omnia intelligit, omnia praecognoscit, atque omnipotens natura cum fit, om- nia potens potest,cui nihil est difficile,nihil impos- sibile, qui tam miranda creauit potentia sua in ve- ritate constituit, ratione perfecit, virtute sustinet, bonitate illustrat, ipsi laus, ipsi honor, ipsi gloria, qui viuit regnat Deus gloriosus excel- sus in saecula saeculorum Amen. AVCTO- AVCTORIS PROTESTATIO ad Caesarem. HAEC sunt Maximiliane Caefar inuictissime, quae mihi ad octo quaestiones, à tua maiestate propositas videbantur dicen- da. Voluisti etenim earundem etiam à me habere iudicium in scriptis, supra ve- ritatem de me faciens aestimationem:qui illis comparandus non sum ingenio, quo- rum ante me sententiam audiuisti. Faciat me venia dignus, si quid minus proprium dixi, quod Imperio celsitudinis tuae via- tor in itinere constitutus, vt potui per in- terualla quod respondendũ occurrebat, dictaui. Dico autem ex mente et amp; manife- stè protestor, me Christianae fidei, synce- rum confessorem, &amp; vnione sacro san- ctae Romanae Ecclesiae vsq́; ad mortẽ velle permanere. Vnde si quid vel in aliis haberetur dictũ vel scriptũ aliter quã illa tenet, sentit, credit et amp; docet, vt verus obediẽtiae filius p̃sentiũ attestatione denũcio, &amp; volo simpliciter esse 7

[unclear] of God, when they behold as the end of their opinion the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, led by the vain talk of secular philosophers, train himself to contempt of God; let no one take away the providence of the supreme and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of, and ungrateful for, the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole world, both visible and invisible, and all and each of the things that are either in heaven or on earth and in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is foreign to his care. For the crops and all the other things that the earth brings forth, and also the storms and the variations of times and the changes of the sky, by which all things that the earth naturally produces grow to maturity, divine providence supplies to the human race; and it provides for all things and each thing, not only the great, but even the very least, to such a degree that not even the slightest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it and rules and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this so great magnitude of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by the one God, who alone exists, he is greatly deceived, and is shown not to know how great is the power of divine might. For indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being can also govern forever, most wisely, what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, can do all things, who alone, omnipotent, created all things.

We therefore, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence, and should also lift up our minds, with whatever strength we can, from those things that are perishable; and, brought back to ourselves, we should be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God, present everywhere. Since it is altogether uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. Yet it does not sustain on one side and surpass on another, nor fill on one side and encompass on another; rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. He is nowhere through the bulk of a body, nowhere absent through his uncircumscribable substance; he is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart. O inexplicable power, O incomprehensible loving-kindness, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity, which does not consist of parts like a body, is not separated by affections like a soul, does not underlie forms like all other things that were made through you, who are in all things, above all things, ruling and governing the universe most wisely.

By these testimonies, therefore, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, it has been sufficiently proved, as I think, that this whole world is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and everlasting, he knows all things, understands all things, foreknows all things; and since he is of an omnipotent nature, being all-powerful, he can do all things. Nothing is difficult for him, nothing impossible; he created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by virtue, illumines them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, God glorious and exalted, forever and ever. Amen.

The Author’s Protestation to the Emperor.

These are the things, most unconquered Caesar Maximilian, that seemed to me necessary to say in response to the eight questions proposed by your majesty. For you wished to have my judgment too, in writing, concerning them, making an estimate of me beyond the truth; for I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before me. Let pardon make me worthy, if I have said anything less appropriate, because, a traveler set upon the road, at the command of your loftiness, I dictated, as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me that should be answered. But I say from my heart and openly declare that I, a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, wish to remain in union with the most holy Roman Church until death. Therefore, if anything should be held to have been said or written, either in these or in other matters, otherwise than that Church holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, as a true son of obedience I declare by the attestation of the present writing, and I simply wish it to be

to be and to be regarded as forever revoked. Therefore, most wise Caesar, I humbly ask and urgently admonish your Majesty that, before you cause my replies to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined and kept, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For the greatest care must be taken that nothing be set before those for whose salvation your Serenity keeps watch, unless it is sound, tested, clear, and lawfully confirmed by the opinion of very many wise men in the Catholic faith. May almighty God by his providence direct and preserve you always, to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neumarkt, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the Christian year one thousand five hundred and eight.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.
